purpose: Explain how sustainability- and climate-related matters are governed, including oversight, decision rights, accountability, reporting lines, and integration with enterprise risk management and core business decision-making, in a manner consistent with IFRS S1/S2 governance disclosure expectations.
tone: Formal, institutional, assurance-oriented and compliance-aligned. Objective and descriptive; emphasizes oversight, accountability, control, and decision-making authority. Avoids promotional language and outcome-claiming.
level_of_detail: Moderate-to-high. Provide enough specificity to evidence governance effectiveness through structure and process (who does what, how often in qualitative terms, how escalation works), while avoiding unnecessary operational minutiae or performance claims.
paragraph_style: Start with a high-level framing paragraph linking sustainability/climate governance to the business model and operations. Progress from principles/ethos to governance mechanics. Use short, topic-led paragraphs; each paragraph covers one governance dimension (mandate, scope, cadence, coordination, capability-building, evaluation). Use role blocks (label + compact responsibility description) for scanability. Introduce visuals/tables with a lead-in sentence and return to narrative that clarifies responsibilities and review processes.
sentence_style: Use precise governance verbs and clear subject-verb-object construction. Prefer multi-clause sentences to enumerate responsibilities in a logical sequence (e.g., propose → validate → approve; monitor → review → report). Use cautious qualifiers for maturity statements (e.g., evolving, in progress, planned) without overcommitting. Use parentheticals sparingly to define generic terms (avoid acronyms unless necessary and defined).
preferred_evidence_style: Evidence through governance mechanics rather than outcomes: (1) governance architecture (diagram/model), (2) formal mandates and delegated authorities, (3) role-to-responsibility mapping and escalation pathways, (4) capability and suitability evidence via structured profiles (genericized), (5) references to documented artifacts (policies, terms of reference, periodic reports) described generically. Use figure/table numbering and descriptive titles for audit-friendly traceability.
table_usage: Use tables as structured evidence artifacts. Preferred tables include: (a) governance body/role-to-responsibility mapping, (b) competency/capability overview for governing bodies (genericized; no personal data), (c) lines-of-defence role comparison. Table titles sit directly above tables and describe purpose (not repeating headings). Cells should contain short narrative snippets (mini-paragraphs) rather than single-word entries.
figure_usage: Use a governance structure diagram to map oversight and decision-making across levels (board-level, executive/management, operational teams, subsidiaries/regions). Show information flow and accountability with directional connectors and relationship labels (e.g., informs, reports to, approves). Optionally incorporate a lines-of-defence concept as an organizing device. Provide a descriptive caption explaining scope and why the figure matters.
pdf_layout_usage: Use a section divider page to signal the chapter. Prefer a two-page rhythm: narrative overview followed by a full-width governance structure figure. Maintain consistent running header/footer with section label and page navigation. Use whitespace to separate narrative blocks from visuals. Place captions adjacent to or below visuals. Where tables and narrative share a page, include a small anchor label/subheading to orient the reader.
how_to_discuss_missing_data: State what information is not available or not disclosed, why (e.g., confidentiality, governance in transition, data not yet centrally captured), and what process exists to improve (e.g., planned formalisation, periodic review of terms of reference, capability-building). Avoid implying completeness where gaps exist; describe interim controls and timelines only in qualitative terms.
what_to_avoid: Company-specific names, acronyms, internal body titles, or branded governance forums
Person names, biographies, career histories, independence classifications tied to individuals, or credential details that identify individuals
Numeric values (including meeting frequencies, years of experience, KPI weights, targets, dates, baselines) and quantified commitments
Jurisdiction-specific regulator names or references that would not generalize
Named tools, vendors, proprietary methodologies, scorecards, or policy/framework titles
Awards, achievements, or qualitative impact claims presented as outcomes
Exact ordering or wording of risk-category lists that could mirror a source document too closely
Overpromising language (e.g., guarantees, ensures outcomes) or promotional adjectives
